## Problem 1
#### Loading and inspecting NY NOAA dataset
```{r}
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")
```

The NY NOAA dataset contains `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations
and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables, representing weather measurements
collected at different stations over time. The variables include
station ID (`id`), observation date (`date`), precipitation (`prcp`),
snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), maximum temperature (`tmax`),
and minimum temperature (`tmin`). The station ID and temperature
variables are stored as character values, the date is stored as a
date variable, and the precipitation and snow measurements are
stored as integers.

The dataset contains `r sum(is.na(ny_noaa))` missing values overall.
Maximum temperature (`tmax`) has `r sum(is.na(ny_noaa$tmax))`
missing observations (`r round(mean(is.na(ny_noaa$tmax)) * 100, 1)`%),
while minimum temperature (`tmin`) has
`r sum(is.na(ny_noaa$tmin))` missing observations
(`r round(mean(is.na(ny_noaa$tmin)) * 100, 1)`%).
In contrast, station ID and date have no missing values.

#### Cleaning the dataset

```{r}
ny_noaa_clean = ny_noaa |> 
  mutate(
    year = year(date), 
    month = month(date),
    day = day(date), 
    prcp = prcp / 10, 
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10, 
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  )
```

#### Snowfall Observations
```{r}
ny_noaa_clean |> 
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |> 
  count(snow) |> 
  arrange(desc(n)) |> 
  slice_head(n =10)
```
The most commonly observed snowfall value is 0 mm, which makes sense because snowfall does not occur every day. The next most common values are 25 mm, 13 mm, and 51 mm, which approximately correspond to 1 inch, 0.5 inches, and 2 inches, respectively. This suggests that some snowfall measurements may have originally been recorded in inches and converted to millimeters.

#### January and July temps over the years

```{r}
ny_noaa_clean |> 
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |> 
  group_by(year, month, id) |> 
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |> 
  filter(!is.na(mean_tmax)) |> 
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month, 
      levels = c(7, 1), 
      labels = c("July", "January")
    )
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax)) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = month),
    alpha = .25,
    size = 0.8
    ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(color = month),
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE, 
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  facet_grid(month ~ ., scales = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  scale_color_viridis_d(
  option = "viridis",
  begin = 0.15,
  end = 0.85
) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Max Temperatures in New York",
    subtitle = "January and July temperatures across weather stations, 1981 - 2010",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Max Temp (°C)",
    caption = "Each point represents one station's monthly average",
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    strip.placement = "outside",
    strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11), 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

This graph shows clear seasonal differences, as shown with consistently higher averages in July as compared to January. The trendline shows a slight increase in January temps from 1981 to 2010, while July temps remain more or less stable. January temps seem to be more variable than July ones. There are potential outliers in January around 1982 and 2004, and in July around 1988 and 2004.

#### Tmax vs Tmin plot

```{r}
ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(tmax), !is.na(tmin)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex() +
  labs(
  title = "Maximum vs Minimum Temperatures",
  subtitle = "Daily temperatures across New York weather stations, 1981–2010",
  x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
  y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)",
  fill = "Observations"
) +
theme_minimal() +
theme(
  plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
  legend.position = "right",
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
)
```
This hexagonal plot shows a strong positive relationship between daily minimum and maximum temperatures across New York weather stations. The highest concentration of observations occurs at the more moderate temperatures, with minimum temperatures around 0–20°C and maximum temperatures around 5–30°C. Some extreme observations are seen, both unusually high and low temperatures, which may suggest outliers or other data-quality issues.

#### Snowfall plot

(ii) make a plot showing the distribution of snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 separately by year.
```{r}
ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow, fill = factor(year))) +
  geom_boxplot(
    alpha = 0.8,
    width = 0.7,
    outlier.size = 1
  ) +
  labs(
  title = "Snowfall Over the Years",
  subtitle = "Snowfall Measured by Weather Stations Between 1981–2010",
  x = "Year",
  y = "Snowfall (mm)"
) +
theme_minimal() +
theme(
  plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
  legend.position = "none",
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1)
)
```
This boxplot shows that the distribution of daily snowfall amounts between 0 and 100 mm was relatively consistent across 1981–2010. The median snowfall was approximately 25 mm in most years, while the middle 50% of observations generally ranged from about 13 to 51 mm. Although some years showed slightly different variability and a few high snowfall outliers, there was no clear overall trend in the median snowfall amount. The similarity across years may partly reflect the concentration of snowfall measurements at common values such as 13, 25, and 51 mm. These results describe snowfall amounts on days with recorded snowfall within the specified range, rather than total annual snowfall.

## Problem 2

#### Load, tidy, merge, and organize
```{r}
demos_df =
  readr::read_csv("nhanes_demos.csv", skip = 4) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex, 
      levels = c(1, 2), 
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
      ),
    education = factor(
      education, 
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c("Less than HS", "HS", "More than HS"),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  ) |> 
  filter(
    age >= 21,
    !is.na(sex),
    !is.na(age),
    !is.na(bmi),
    !is.na(education)
  )

acc_data_df = 
  readr::read_csv("nhanes_accel.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names()

nhanes_df = demos_df |> 
  left_join(acc_data_df, by = "seqn") |> 
  mutate(seqn = as.character(seqn))
```
The merged NHANES dataset contains `r nrow(nhanes_df)` participants and
`r ncol(nhanes_df)` variables. The dataset combines demographic information along with with 1,440 minute-level accelerometer activity measurements per participant. Participants younger than 21 years of age and those with missing demographic information were excluded. Categorical variables were converted to factors, with education treated as an ordered factor. The datasets were merged using the unique participant identifier (`seqn`) through a left join, preserving all eligible participants from the demographic dataset.

#### Men's and Women's Education
```{r}
nhanes_df |> 
  count(sex, education) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex, 
    values_from = n
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    Total = Male + Female
  ) |> 
  janitor::adorn_totals("row") |> 
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Education Level", "Male", "Female", "Total")
  )
```
#### Distribution of Age by Sex and Education
```{r}
nhanes_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = education, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(
  begin = 0.45,
  end = 0.88
) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education Level",
    x = "Education Level",
    y = "Age"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    strip.placement = "outside",
    strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11), 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

Among the 228 participants, the largest education category was More than HS, representing approximately `r round(115 / 228 * 100, 1)`% of the sample. Overall, the sample contained 118 men and 110 women, indicating a relatively even distribution by sex. The largest difference in counts between men and women occurred in the high school education category, where `r round(mean(nhanes_df$education[nhanes_df$sex == "Male"] == "HS") * 100, 1)`% men had a high school education compared to `r round(mean(nhanes_df$education[nhanes_df$sex == "Female"] == "HS") * 100, 1)`% of women.

From the boxplot, participants with more than a high school education generally appeared younger than those with less than a high school education. Among participants with a high school education, women had a median age of `r median(nhanes_df$age[nhanes_df$sex == "Female" & nhanes_df$education == "HS"])`
years, compared with `r median(nhanes_df$age[nhanes_df$sex == "Male" & nhanes_df$education == "HS"])`
years for men. Although median ages differed across groups, the age distributions overlapped considerably, indicating variability within each education category.

#### Total Activity
```{r}
nhanes_df |> 
  mutate(
    total_activity = rowSums(pick(min1:min1440), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |> 
  
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = sex),
    alpha = .4,
    size = 1.5
    ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE, 
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ education, nrow = 1) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(
  begin = 0.15,
  end = 0.89
) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age, Sex and Education Level",
    x = "Age (Years)",
    y = "Total Accelerometer Data (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

```
These plots show that total daily activity generally decreased with age across all three education categories for both men and women. The steepest decline was observed among participants with less than a high school education, while those with more than a high school education showed a more gradual decline. Among participants with a high school education or higher, women generally had higher predicted activity levels than men across the age range. Despite these patterns, there is variability in activity levels within each education category, and we can't really predict anything about age, sex, and education in relation to daily activity.

#### Activity, Education, and Sex
```{r}
nhanes_long_df = nhanes_df |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = min1:min1440, 
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    names_transform = list(minute = as.integer),
    values_to = "activity"    
  ) |> 
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |> 
  summarise(
    mean_activity = mean(activity, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) 

nhanes_long_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(
    x = minute / 60, 
    y = mean_activity, 
    color = sex
    )) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    span = 0.1,
    se = FALSE,
    linewiddth = 0.7
  ) + 
  facet_wrap(~ education, nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 4)) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(
    begin = 0.15,
    end = 0.75
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity Patterns by Sex and Education Level",
    x = "Time of Day (Hours)",
    y = "Mean Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), 
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```
Across all education levels, activity was lowest during the early morning hours, increased sharply after 6 AM, and declined in the evening. Men and women showed similar daily patterns, although women generally had higher daytime activity levels, particularly among participants with a high school education or higher. Participants with less than a high school education had the highest midday activity peaks. Overall, activity patterns were similar across education levels, with some differences by sex.
